title: Steadying Yourself Through Change
description: For anyone going through a move, a new job, a breakup, a new baby, retirement or any big shift. Each day is one small way to find steady ground, keep a few anchors in place, and give yourself time to adjust.
tasks: Write one sentence that names the big change you are in right now, plainly, as if telling a kind friend.
Pick two or three anchors to keep steady this season, such as a morning coffee, an evening walk or a Sunday call, and write them on a sticky note.
Make two short lists side by side: what is changing in your life and what is staying the same.
Drink a full glass of water before you check any messages this morning.
Take a ten minute walk at the same time you usually would, even if the route is new.
List three things you miss about the way life was before this change.
List three things you are quietly hoping for on the other side of this change.
Tell yourself out loud, once today, that adjusting takes time and you are allowed to be in the middle.
Find one coffee shop, bakery or diner near where you spend most of your day and sit there for fifteen minutes.
Put one familiar object, a mug, a photo or a blanket, somewhere you will see it first thing in the morning.
Send a short text to someone from before the change, just to say you were thinking of them.
Write down one practical task you could use help with this week, then name one person who might help.
Choose the single next step on your plate and do only that step today.
Notice one small thing that went well today in your new situation and say it to yourself.
Eat one meal today at a table, without a screen, the way you might have before things shifted.
Go to bed within fifteen minutes of your usual time tonight, wherever you are sleeping now.
Name one feeling about this change that seems to contradict another one, and let both be true for a minute.
Spend five minutes looking out a window and notice what the light is doing outside.
Learn the name of one person you see regularly in your new routine, a neighbor, a cashier or a coworker.
Write a note to yourself that begins, "It makes sense that this is hard because..." and finish it honestly.
Wake up and do the same first three things you did before the change, in the same order.

Look up the nearest public library and find out its hours.
Unpack, sort or put away one box, bag or drawer, and stop there.
Call someone who knew you before this change and ask how their week is going.

Pick a spot for your keys, wallet and phone and use it every time today.
When a worry about the future comes up today, write it down and then write the one thing you can do next about it.
Stand outside for two minutes this evening and notice the temperature, the sounds and the sky.
Hang up or prop up one picture that makes the space feel a little more like yours.
Make a short playlist of songs that remind you of who you were before this change.
Choose one small new routine to learn this week and write down exactly when it will happen.
If today feels heavy, cancel or postpone one thing that is not essential and rest instead.
Write a short goodbye note to something that has ended, a home, a job or a way of life, and keep it or tear it up.
Take a different street on a familiar errand and notice one thing you had not seen before.
Ask a neighbor or coworker for one local recommendation, a good park, a reliable mechanic or the best tacos.
Set out tomorrow's clothes tonight so the morning has one less decision in it.
Write down what a good enough day looks like during this transition, then aim for that, not a perfect one.
Spend ten minutes in a park, courtyard or green patch near you and notice three living things.
Give one part of your new space a job, a reading corner, a charging spot or a place for mail.
Put a recurring reminder in your calendar to check in with one old friend every two weeks.
Make a list of the paperwork or logistics this change has created and circle just one to handle today.
Before you get out of bed, take three slow breaths and name one thing you can count on today.
Notice one strength this change is asking you to use, patience, courage or flexibility, and write it down.
Plan one simple meal you can cook on autopilot when you are tired, and buy what you need for it.
Light a candle, play soft music or open a window when you get home to mark the end of the day.
Tell one trusted person how you are really doing with this change, in two honest sentences.
Find the nearest place to buy groceries that you like, and walk its aisles slowly once.
Write the date at the top of a page and describe where you are in this change today, so you can look back later.
Choose one evening this week to be completely unscheduled and protect it.
Say no to one extra commitment today so you have room to settle.
Keep a small notebook by your bed and write one line in it tonight about how today felt.
